Cholesky, SVD and Least Squares

Three factorizations of one return matrix: a projection that rebuilds TAIEX from its sectors, a decomposition that measures rank and conditioning, and a triangular factor that whitens returns.

Volume II · Linear Algebra for PortfoliosBuilds on LM2 · LM4 · LM5 · LM7 · LM8 · LM9 · LM10 · LM11Leads to LM16 · LM18 · LM23 · LM27 · LM30 · LM32Time ≈ 3 h + labPDF A4 print edition
Learning Outcomes
MasteryAfter this module you should be able to:
1derive the normal equations from the orthogonality of the residual, and compute least-squares fits, projection matrices and R-squared
2explain why TAIEX's daily returns are almost an exact combination of its sector indices' returns, and why the fitted coefficients are not sector weights
3derive the singular value decomposition from the eigen-decomposition of M⊤M, and relate it to principal components and condition numbers
4compute the minimum-norm solution of a rank-deficient least-squares problem with the pseudoinverse, and state a numerical rank with its tolerance and scale
5compute a Cholesky factor by recursion, and interpret its entries as the slopes and residual standard deviations of sequential regressions
6whiten and colour returns with a Cholesky factor, and explain why whitened returns have a mean squared length equal to the number of assets
7apply lstsq, pinv, svd, matrix_rank, cond and cholesky in NumPy, and label each result as descriptive, in-sample or a stability check
Learning Module Overview
  • Least squares projects a response on the column space of the design. The residual is orthogonal to every column, which gives the normal equations X⊤Xβ^​=X⊤y; with an intercept, R-squared is cos2θ.
  • TAIEX's last 250 daily returns, fitted on the returns of 28 sector indices, give R-squared 0.99912 and a Semiconductor coefficient of 0.542. The fit rests on an accounting identity with drifting weights: the coefficients are the constant mix that best reproduces the window, not the sector weights.
  • Fitted year by year, Semiconductor's coefficient rose from 0.189 in 2009 to 0.554 in 2026. Every year's R-squared is at least 0.99800, while one constant mix for the full sample reaches only 0.98333.
  • Every matrix factors as USV⊤. For data, X~/T​=USV⊤ gives Σ^=VS2V⊤, so λk​=sk2​, and forming X~⊤X~ squares the condition number: 10.40 becomes 108.09 for the 28 sectors.
  • December 2008 has 22 returns for 29 coefficients: rank 22, a null space of dimension 7 and an exact fit of any response. The pseudoinverse picks the minimum-norm fit, and the fit stays exact without Semiconductor.
  • Numerical rank depends on the tolerance and the scale. Electronic and its eight sub-industries have rank 9 at δ=0.01 over the full sample and 8 in 2016, while matrix_rank reports 9 in every year.
  • A positive definite Σ^ factors uniquely as LL⊤, a chain of regressions. Whitened returns zt​=L−1(Rt​−Rˉ) have identity covariance and a mean squared length of exactly N.
  • For five sectors, 7 April 2025 has ∥zt​∥2=89.30, the largest of 4,382 days, in either asset order; the 10% daily limit capped that day's returns, so even this figure understates the shock.

1Introduction

Volume II has built vectors (LM8), linear systems (LM9), covariance matrices (LM10) and eigenvectors (LM11). This module closes the volume with three factorizations that software uses every day. Least squares splits a response into a fitted part and a residual orthogonal to it. The singular value decomposition (SVD) measures rank and conditioning on the data matrix itself. The Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix turns correlated returns into uncorrelated ones.

Motivating CaseCan you rebuild TAIEX from its sectors?

A desk analyst wants to know how much of TAIEX moves with semiconductors, without a file of index weights. FinMind serves daily closes of 30 TWSE sector indices, and 28 of them contain no other sector index. She regresses TAIEX's last 250 daily returns, 25 September 2025 to 8 October 2026, on the returns of these 28 sectors, with an intercept.

The fit reproduces TAIEX almost perfectly: R-squared (Section 2) is 0.99912. The coefficient on Semiconductor is 0.542, on ElectronicPartsComponents 0.098, on FinancialInsurance 0.084 and on ComputerPeripheralEquipment 0.054. The 28 coefficients sum to 0.990 (Exhibit 1).

A colleague runs the same regression on the 22 daily returns of December 2008. That fit is exact, with R-squared 1, and it stays exact when the Semiconductor column is removed. Which fit tells more, and why is the perfect one worthless?

Section 2 treats least squares as a projection, and Section 3 applies it to the case. Section 4 derives the SVD. Section 5 handles rank deficiency and resolves the case, and Section 6 builds the Cholesky factor and whitens real returns.

NoteNotation for this module

Returns are daily simple returns of price indices. The sample is 2 December 2008 → 8 October 2026, T=4,382 returns (a count), unless a sub-sample is named. U28 is the 28 leaf indices among the 30 TWSE sector indices that FinMind serves daily. A leaf index contains no other sector index, so U28 excludes the aggregates Electronic and ChemicalBiotechnologyMedicalCare. S3 is Semiconductor, FinancialInsurance and Food; S5 adds Plastics and ShippingTransportation, in that order.

Local symbols: yt​ TAIEX's return, yˉ​ its mean, y~​=y−yˉ​1, (1 X) the design with an intercept, α^ the intercept, x a single column, MVi,t​ the market value of index member i; mij​ and kij​ the entries of matrices M and K; uk​ and vk​ the columns of U and V, k the index of sk​ and λk​, sk​ the singular values (not the standard deviations si​ of LM8 and LM10), M+ the pseudoinverse, κ(M)=s1​/sN​, δ a rank tolerance, colM and nullM the column space and null space, xh​ a vector of nullM; L the lower-triangular Cholesky factor, Σ^=LL⊤ (this module has no leverage), lij​ its entries, p their summation index (not m, which names entries of M), dj​ the pivots of LM9 and LM10, σ^ij​ the entries of Σ^ and zt​=L−1(Rt​−Rˉ) the whitened returns, with entries zj,t​; σ12​, σ12​ and σ22​ the entries of LM7's annualized covariance matrix of 0050 and 00679B (Problems 9 and 10). Each vk​ is signed so that its entry largest in absolute value is positive (the first of tied entries), and uk​=Mvk​/sk​. Moments divide by T, as in LM10.

NoteResearch hygiene

The editor fixed U28, S3 and S5 before this module was written. Every fit here is in-sample: an R-squared near 1 comes from an accounting identity, not from a forecast. The yearly fits are a stability check, not an out-of-sample test. The SVD, L and zt​ use the full-sample Σ^, so they are descriptive: the most unusual day is judged with data from later years.

2Least Squares as a Projection

derive the normal equations from the orthogonality of the residual, and compute least-squares fits, projection matrices and R-squared

Least squares is geometry before it is algebra, so start with one column in the plane.

Example 1The closest multiple of one vector

Find the multiple βx of x=(2,1)⊤ that is closest to y=(1,3)⊤, its residual and the distance.

Solution

The multiples of x form a line through the origin (Exhibit 2). The point of the line closest to y is the foot of the perpendicular, so the residual must be orthogonal to x: x⊤(y−βx)=0. Hence β^​=x⊤y/x⊤x=5/5=1.

The fitted vector is y^​=(2,1)⊤, and the residual is ε^=y−y^​=(−1,2)⊤, with x⊤ε^=−2+2=0. The distance is ∥ε^∥=5​=2.236. Every other multiple is farther away: 1.5x lies at distance 2.5. LM8 found the same closest multiple in its proof of (8.6), with the roles of the two vectors exchanged.

The normal equations

Now let X be any T×N matrix with columns x1​,…,xN​. Its column space colX is the set of all combinations Xβ=β1​x1​+⋯+βN​xN​ (LM9). Least squares finds the point of colX closest to a response y (Strang 2016, §4.2). It minimizes ∥y−Xβ∥2, the sum of the squared misses over the T rows.

TheoremLeast squares

Let X be a T×N matrix and y a vector in RT. A vector β^​ minimizes ∥y−Xβ∥2 if and only if its residual ε^:=y−Xβ^​ is orthogonal to every column of X:

X⊤ε^=0,that is,X⊤Xβ^​=X⊤y.(12.1)
When X has full column rank, the minimizer is unique: β^​=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.

Proof. Suppose that X⊤ε^=0, and take any β. Then y−Xβ=ε^+X(β^​−β) is a sum of two orthogonal vectors, and Pythagoras gives

∥y−Xβ∥2=∥ε^∥2+∥X(β^​−β)∥2≥∥ε^∥2.

Conversely, expand the squared length and differentiate with the rules of LM10:

∥y−Xβ∥2=y⊤y−2β⊤X⊤y+β⊤X⊤Xβ,∇β​∥y−Xβ∥2=2X⊤Xβ−2X⊤y.​

The gradient vanishes at any minimizer (LM7), which is (12.1). With full column rank, X⊤X is positive definite (LM10), hence invertible. ■

The theorem names the fitted values y^​:=Xβ^​, the point of colX closest to y. Equations (12.1) are the normal equations, "normal" meaning perpendicular. Section 5 shows that they have a solution even without full column rank.

The projection matrix

With full column rank, y^​=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤y, so one matrix sends every response to its fitted values:

Π:=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤,Π⊤=Π=Π2,trΠ=N.​(12.2)

The projection matrix Π is symmetric, by the rule (MK)⊤=K⊤M⊤ of LM8 and because the inverse of the symmetric matrix X⊤X is symmetric. It is idempotent, Π2=Π, because the middle factor X⊤X of Π2 cancels one inverse: projecting twice changes nothing. Its trace counts the columns. For two matrices whose products KM and MK are both square, the trace is cyclic, tr(KM)=∑i​∑j​kij​mji​=tr(MK). Here kij​ and mij​ are the entries of K and M. Hence

trΠ=tr((X⊤X)−1X⊤X)=trIN​=N.

The residual is ε^=(I−Π)y, and I−Π projects on the directions orthogonal to every column.

The intercept and R-squared

A fit with an intercept uses the design (1 X), whose first column is 1. Its first normal equation, 1⊤ε^=0, says that the residuals sum to zero. Averaging y=α^1+Xβ^​+ε^ over the rows therefore gives yˉ​=α^+Rˉ⊤β^​, and subtracting leaves y~​=X~β^​+ε^. The other normal equations, X⊤ε^=0, combine with the first into X~⊤ε^=0. Substituting ε^=y~​−X~β^​ and dividing by T:

Σ^β^​=T1​X~⊤y~​,α^=yˉ​−Rˉ⊤β^​.(12.3)

The slopes depend only on covariances, and the intercept on the means and the slopes.

Centring splits y~​ into two orthogonal pieces, the centred fit X~β^​=y^​−yˉ​1 and the residual. R-squared is the share of the centred response's squared length that the fit reproduces (LM23 treats it as a statistic). By Pythagoras,

R-squared​:=1−∥y~​∥2∥ε^∥2​=∥y~​∥2∥y^​−yˉ​1∥2​=cos2θ,​(12.4)

where θ is the angle between y~​ and the centred fit (LM8). With one column, cosθ is the absolute value of the sample correlation of x and y, so R-squared is the squared correlation.

Example 2A line through four points

Fit y=α^1+β^​x+ε^ to x=(0,1,2,3)⊤ and y=(1,3,2,6)⊤. Check (12.1), and compute R-squared in two ways.

Solution

The means are 1.5 and 3, so x~=(−1.5,−0.5,0.5,1.5)⊤ and y~​=(−2,0,−1,3)⊤. By (12.3), β^​=x~⊤y~​/x~⊤x~=7/5=1.4 and α^=3−1.4×1.5=0.9.

The fitted values are (0.9,2.3,3.7,5.1)⊤ and the residuals (0.1,0.7,−1.7,0.9)⊤. The residuals sum to zero, and x⊤ε^=0+0.7−3.4+2.7=0, as (12.1) requires.

The squared lengths are ∥ε^∥2=4.2 and ∥y~​∥2=14, so R-squared is 1−4.2/14=0.7. As a squared cosine it is (x~⊤y~​)2/(∥x~∥2∥y~​∥2)=49/70=0.7.

PitfallWithout an intercept, R-squared is another number

Formula (12.4) needs 1⊤ε^=0, which only an intercept guarantees. Fit Example 2's data through the origin instead: β^​=25/14=1.786 and ∥ε^∥2=5.357, a worse fit than 4.2. Yet the uncentred share 1−∥ε^∥2/∥y∥2=1−5.357/50=0.893 exceeds 0.7. The centred formula gives 0.617, and no angle stands behind it. Compare fits by their residuals, and quote R-squared only for fits with an intercept.

Knowledge Check 1

In Example 1 the residual is orthogonal to the fitted vector. Why does the theorem demand orthogonality to every column of X, not only to y^​?

Answer

Orthogonality to the fitted vector alone also holds at bad points. At β=0 the fit is 0, and every residual is orthogonal to 0, yet the distance ∥y∥=10​=3.162 exceeds the minimum 5​. If a column has xj⊤​ε^=0, the gradient is not zero, and a small step along that column shortens the residual.

3Reading TAIEX from Its Sectors

explain why TAIEX's daily returns are almost an exact combination of its sector indices' returns, and why the fitted coefficients are not sector weights

Before reading the case's coefficients, consider why such a fit can be nearly exact.

The index identity

TWSE computes TAIEX as the total market value of its member stocks divided by a base value, times the base level (TWSE IndexS02). It computes the sector indices the same way (TWSE IndexS03). Suppose nothing but prices changes between two closes, so that the market value MVi,t​ of member i grows by its return, MVi,t​=MVi,t−1​(1+Ri,t​). With the same base value on both days,

1+yt​=∑i​MVi,t−1​∑i​MVi,t​​=i∑​wi,t−1​(1+Ri,t​),wi,t−1​:=∑j​MVj,t−1​MVi,t−1​​.​

So TAIEX's return is a weighted average of its members' returns, wt−1⊤​Rt​ as in LM8, with weights set at the previous close. The same identity holds inside each sector index. Suppose every member of TAIEX belongs to exactly one of the 28 sectors. Grouping the members by sector then turns TAIEX's return into an average of sector returns, weighted by the sectors' market values at the previous close.

Two things break the identity: members or share counts that change, which alter the base value, and members outside the 28 sectors. TWSE added four sector indices with base date 30 June 2023 (綠能環保類, 數位雲端類, 運動休閒類 and 居家生活類; TWSE IndexS03). FinMind serves no daily series for them, so from July 2023, which includes the whole last-250 window, some TAIEX members lie outside U28.

A third thing, weights that drift every day with relative prices, leaves the identity intact. The drift keeps any constant mix from reproducing the identity. The coefficients of a fit are therefore the constant weights that best reproduce TAIEX's daily moves in the window, never "the sector weights".

Example 3Resolving the case: the last 250 returns

Fit TAIEX's last 250 daily returns on the 28 sector returns with an intercept, and read the coefficients.

Solution

The design (1 X) is 250×29 with full column rank, so (12.1) has one solution. R-squared is 0.99912: the fit reproduces 99.912% of the centred response's squared length. Semiconductor's coefficient is 0.542, followed by ElectronicPartsComponents 0.098, FinancialInsurance 0.084, ComputerPeripheralEquipment 0.054, OtherElectronic 0.047 and CommunicationsInternet 0.038 (Exhibit 3).

The 28 coefficients sum to 0.990, and the intercept is −0.013% a day; this module does not explain either number. Seven coefficients are negative, the smallest −0.0081 (InformationService). A market value cannot be negative, so these coefficients are not weights: they are fitting noise among correlated columns.

Semiconductor matters most: without its column, R-squared falls to 0.856. So the analyst's answer describes the window: a constant mix with 0.542 in Semiconductor reproduced TAIEX's daily moves best.

Example 4One fit per year

Repeat the fit on each calendar year from 2009 to 2026 (to 8 October) and on the full sample. How stable are the coefficients, and how good is each fit?

Solution

Semiconductor's coefficient rises from 0.189 in 2009 to 0.554 in 2026, and FinancialInsurance's falls from 0.133 to 0.080 (Exhibit 4). Every year's R-squared is at least 0.99800, the value of 2021. The full sample, one constant mix for almost 18 years, reaches only 0.98333. A constant mix cannot follow coefficients that drift this much, so the full-sample fit is worse than every yearly fit.

The comparison is a stability check. It shows how the best-reproducing mix changed; it does not show how well any mix predicts.

The widget compares the 28 coefficients of any two samples: a calendar year, the last 250 returns or the full sample.

導讀最小平方法：投影，不是權重

最小平方法（least squares）把 y 投影（projection）到設計矩陣（design matrix）的行空間（column space）上：殘差（residual）必須和每一行都正交（orthogonal），這就是正規方程（normal equations）。加上截距（intercept）以後，判定係數（R-squared）等於中心化（centring）後的 y 與中心化配適值（fitted value）夾角（angle）餘弦（cosine）的平方。加權股價指數的報酬本來就是成分股報酬的市值加權平均，所以對 28 個類股指數迴歸（regression），判定係數幾乎是 1；這是會計恆等式（accounting identity），不是預測能力。係數是「這段期間最能重現大盤每日漲跌的固定權重」，不是類股市值權重：真正的權重每天隨股價漂移，而且有七個係數是負的。逐年重做時半導體的係數從 0.189 升到 0.554，這是穩定性檢查（stability check），不是樣本外檢定（out-of-sample test）。

Knowledge Check 2

Why can a least-squares coefficient be slightly negative when every sector's market-value weight is positive?

Answer

Least squares minimizes the squared misses and imposes no sign. The true weights drift, and correlated columns such as the electronics sub-industries partly substitute for one another. A small negative coefficient can therefore lower the sum of squared residuals. In the last 250 returns, seven coefficients are negative, the smallest −0.0081 (InformationService).

4The Singular Value Decomposition

derive the singular value decomposition from the eigen-decomposition of M⊤M, and relate it to principal components and condition numbers

LM11 decomposed the symmetric matrix Σ^. The SVD decomposes a rectangular data matrix directly.

From a circle to an ellipse

An invertible 2×2 matrix maps the unit circle to an ellipse. For

M=(4−2​44​),

the ellipse has semi-axes of lengths 6 and 4 (Exhibit 5). Two perpendicular unit vectors, v1​ and v2​, map onto the axes: Mvk​=sk​uk​, where u1​ and u2​ are perpendicular unit vectors and s1​=6, s2​=4. So M=USV⊤ acts in three steps: V⊤ carries each vk​ to a coordinate axis, S stretches the axes by sk​, and U carries them to the uk​.

The decomposition

Let M be a real T×N matrix. The matrix M⊤M is symmetric and positive semidefinite, since β⊤M⊤Mβ=∥Mβ∥2≥0 for every β. By the spectral theorem of LM11, it has orthonormal eigenvectors v1​,…,vN​ with eigenvalues λ1​≥⋯≥λN​≥0. Set sk​:=λk​​ and, when sk​>0, uk​:=Mvk​/sk​. These vectors are orthonormal:

uj⊤​uk​​=sj​sk​vj⊤​M⊤Mvk​​=sj​sk​λk​vj⊤​vk​​={1,0,​j=k,j=k.​​

When sk​=0, ∥Mvk​∥2=λk​=0, so Mvk​=0. Because the vk​ form an orthonormal basis, M=∑k​Mvk​vk⊤​, and only the terms with sk​>0 survive.

TheoremSingular value decomposition

Let M be a real T×N matrix, with singular values s1​≥s2​≥⋯≥0 (the square roots of the eigenvalues of M⊤M) and orthonormal eigenvectors vk​ of M⊤M. Then

M=sk​>0∑​sk​uk​vk⊤​,uk​=Mvk​/sk​,
where the uk​ are orthonormal in RT and the number of positive sk​ is rankM. When rankM=N, stacking the pieces gives the thin SVD M=USV⊤: U is T×N with U⊤U=IN​, S=diag(s1​,…,sN​) and V is orthogonal.

The number of positive sk​ is the rank, because Mβ=∑sk​>0​sk​(vk⊤​β)uk​ ranges over the span of those uk​ (Strang 2016, ch. 7).

Example 5The SVD of a 2×2 matrix

Compute the SVD of the matrix M above by hand.

Solution

First,

M⊤M=(208​832​),
with trace 52 and determinant 576. By LM11's 2×2 formula, the eigenvalues are 26±262−576​=26±10: λ1​=36 and λ2​=16, so s1​=6 and s2​=4.

For λ1​=36 the first row of M⊤M−36I is (−16,8), so v1​=(1,2)⊤/5​. Orthogonality and the sign rule give v2​=(2,−1)⊤/5​. Then u1​=Mv1​/6=(2,1)⊤/5​ and u2​=Mv2​/4=(1,−2)⊤/5​.

Check: ∣detM∣=∣16+8∣=24=s1​s2​, because the orthogonal factors have determinants ±1.

Principal components from the data matrix

Apply the SVD to the centred data matrix, scaled by 1/T​:

T​X~​=USV⊤⟹Σ^=TX~⊤X~​=VS2V⊤.(12.5)

Compare LM11's Σ^=QΛQ⊤. The eigenvalues are the squared singular values, λk​=sk2​. When the eigenvalues are distinct, the right singular vectors are the principal directions, vk​=qk​ under the same sign rule. The SVD also gives the score series: X~vk​=T​sk​uk​. This route never forms X~⊤X~, which matters for accuracy.

Conditioning

For a matrix of full column rank, the condition number is κ(M):=s1​/sN​. On a symmetric positive definite matrix the singular values are the eigenvalues, so κ agrees with LM11's λ1​/λN​. Because X~⊤X~=TVS2V⊤,

κ(X~⊤X~)=κ(Σ^)=sN2​s12​​=κ(X~)2.(12.6)

The normal equations work with X~⊤X~, so they square the condition number. Floating-point arithmetic carries about 16 significant digits (LM2), so rounding changes a matrix by a relative amount of order 10−16. By LM11's bound (11.9), such a change in a positive definite matrix moves the solution by a relative amount of at most about κ×10−16. Hence, as a rule of thumb, a condition number κ can cost about log10​κ of the 16 digits.

np.linalg.lstsq works on the matrix it is given and returns that matrix's singular values (NumPy reference). A call on X~ therefore never squares κ(X~) by forming X~⊤X~. When the residual is small, the accuracy of its slopes depends on κ(X~) rather than on κ(X~)2.

Example 6Conditioning of the 28 sectors

Compute the extreme singular values of X~/T​ for U28 on the full sample, and the condition numbers of X~ and Σ^. Repeat for the last 250 returns.

Solution

The largest singular value is s1​=0.054245 and the smallest is s28​=0.005218, so κ(X~)=10.40. By (12.6), κ(Σ^)=108.09 from the unrounded ratio, the figure LM11 finds from the eigenvalues. On the last 250 returns, κ(X~)=17.04 and κ(X~⊤X~)=290.2.

Both are small, and Exhibit 6 shows that lstsq and the normal equations agree to better than 10−14.

Knowledge Check 3

A 2×2 matrix M has singular values 5 and 0.5. What are its condition number and the absolute value of its determinant? What are they for M⊤M?

Answer

The condition number is 5/0.5=10 and ∣detM∣=5×0.5=2.5. The matrix M⊤M has eigenvalues 25 and 0.25, so its condition number is 100, the square of 10, and its determinant is 6.25.

5Rank Deficiency, Numerical Rank and the Pseudoinverse

compute the minimum-norm solution of a rank-deficient least-squares problem with the pseudoinverse, and state a numerical rank with its tolerance and scale
apply lstsq, pinv, svd, matrix_rank, cond and cholesky in NumPy, and label each result as descriptive, in-sample or a stability check

More coefficients than returns

December 2008 has 22 daily returns, and the design (1 X) has 29 columns. Its rank is at most 22, and NumPy finds exactly 22, so by (9.7) of LM9 the null space has dimension 29−22=7. The columns then span all of R22: every response, TAIEX or not, is fitted exactly. R-squared is 1 by arithmetic, not by evidence.

The normal equations then have infinitely many solutions, because adding a vector of the null space changes no fitted value. They form LM9's particular solution plus null space, and software needs a rule to pick one.

The pseudoinverse

TheoremMinimum-norm least squares

Let M be a real T×N matrix with the SVD of Section 4, and let y be in RT. Define the pseudoinverse

M+:=sk​>0∑​sk​1​vk​uk⊤​.(12.7)
In matrix form M+=VS−1U⊤, where U, S and V keep only the positive singular values and their vectors. Then M+y solves the normal equations M⊤Mβ=M⊤y, and every other solution has a larger norm.

The vector M+y solves the normal equations. Transposing the theorem of Section 4 gives M⊤=∑sk​>0​sk​vk​uk⊤​, and the orthonormal uk​ then give M⊤M=∑sk​>0​sk2​vk​vk⊤​. Since the vk​ are orthonormal too,

M⊤MM+y=sk​>0∑​sk​vk​uk⊤​y=M⊤y.

At full column rank, M+=(M⊤M)−1M⊤ gives the unique solution of Section 2.

Deep DiveWhy M+y has the smallest normoptional · click to expand

Two solutions of the normal equations differ by a vector xh​ with M⊤Mxh​=0, so ∥Mxh​∥2=xh⊤​M⊤Mxh​=0. By Section 4, Mxh​=∑sk​>0​sk​(vk⊤​xh​)uk​ vanishes exactly when xh​ is orthogonal to every vk​ with sk​>0. The vector M+y is a combination of these vk​, so it is orthogonal to xh​, and Pythagoras gives

∥M+y+xh​∥2=∥M+y∥2+∥xh​∥2.
Every other solution is longer, and M+y is the only solution orthogonal to nullM.

Example 7December 2008: two exact fits

Fit TAIEX's 22 daily returns of December 2008 on the 28 sectors with an intercept. Compare the minimum-norm solution with the minimum-norm fit after deleting Semiconductor's column.

Solution

The design is 22×29 with rank 22, so every fit is exact. np.linalg.lstsq and np.linalg.pinv both return the minimum-norm solution (12.7). Its Semiconductor coefficient is 0.145, FinancialInsurance's is 0.165, and the norm of all 29 coefficients is 0.285 (Exhibit 7).

Deleting Semiconductor leaves a 22×28 design, still of rank 22, so the fit stays exact. Its minimum-norm solution moves FinancialInsurance to 0.218, with norm 0.401. The two exact fits disagree on every coefficient. As LM9's three-day fits showed, an exact fit carries no evidence about weights; this answers the case's second question.

Numerical rank

In exact arithmetic the rank is the number of non-zero singular values. Floating-point arithmetic keeps about 16 significant digits (LM2), so a singular value that is zero in exact arithmetic is computed as a number of order 10−16s1​. Software therefore counts the singular values above a tolerance: the numerical rank at tolerance δ is the number of sk​>δs1​. By default, np.linalg.matrix_rank uses δ=max(T,N)×2.2×10−16, and np.linalg.pinv treats every sk​≤10−15s1​ as zero (NumPy reference).

Such a tolerance answers a question about arithmetic, not about data. LM11 found Electronic nearly a combination of its eight sub-industries, a relation that a tolerance near 10−15 cannot see. That near-dependence is why U28 excludes the aggregates: adding Electronic raises κ(X~) from 10.40 to 48.33, and to 642.0 in 2016 (Exhibit 6).

Example 8Electronic and its eight sub-industries

Standardize the daily returns of Electronic and its eight sub-industries (divisor T), and divide the standardized matrix by T​. Find its numerical rank at δ=0.1 and at δ=0.01, on the full sample and in 2016.

Solution

On the full sample the smallest singular value is s9​=0.0346s1​, and in 2016 it is 0.00277s1​ (Exhibit 8). At δ=0.01 the numerical rank is therefore 9 on the full sample and 8 in 2016; at δ=0.1 it is 8 in both. matrix_rank reports 9 in every calendar year.

Scale matters too: for the centred returns without standardizing (the covariance scale), the full-sample ratio is 0.0329 instead of 0.0346. A numerical rank needs both its tolerance and its scale.

Pitfall"Full rank" is not "well determined"

np.linalg.matrix_rank reports 9 for Electronic and its sub-industries in every year, yet in 2016 the smallest singular value is 0.3% of the largest. Coefficients on such nearly dependent columns move a lot when the data move a little (LM11). Report sN​/s1​ or κ next to any rank, and choose δ for the precision of the data, not of the computer.

The calls of this section, on the December 2008 design:

Python
import numpy as np

# X: 22 x 28 sector returns of December 2008; y: TAIEX's 22 returns
design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), X])       # (1 X), 22 x 29
b_lstsq = np.linalg.lstsq(design, y, rcond=None)[0]   # minimum norm
b_pinv = np.linalg.pinv(design) @ y                   # the same, (12.7)
# s comes in descending order, and the rows of Vh are the v_k
U, s, Vh = np.linalg.svd(design, full_matrices=False)
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(design))                  # 22
print(np.abs(b_lstsq - b_pinv).max() < 1e-12)         # True
導讀奇異值分解與數值秩

奇異值分解（singular value decomposition）把任何矩陣寫成「正交變換（orthogonal transformation，即旋轉或鏡射）、沿座標軸伸縮、再一次正交變換」：可逆（invertible）的 2×2 矩陣把單位圓映成橢圓，奇異值（singular value）就是橢圓的半軸長。把報酬矩陣中心化（centring）並除以 T​，對 X~/T​ 做奇異值分解，樣本共變異數矩陣（sample covariance matrix）的特徵值（eigenvalue）就等於奇異值的平方；特徵值互不相同時，右奇異向量（right singular vector）就是主成分（principal component）方向。正規方程（normal equations）先算 X~⊤X~，會把條件數（condition number）平方，所以軟體直接在 X~ 上計算。2008 年 12 月只有 22 個報酬，卻有 29 個係數，秩（rank）只有 22，任何反應變數（response）都能完全配適，判定係數（R-squared）等於 1 只是算術結果。擬反矩陣（pseudoinverse）從無限多組解中挑出範數（norm）最小的一組；拿掉半導體一樣完全配適，係數卻全變了。數值秩（numerical rank）取決於容許誤差（tolerance）與尺度（scale），matrix_rank 說「滿秩（full rank）」不代表係數估得準。

Knowledge Check 4

A 22×29 design M has rank 22. How many exact solutions do the normal equations have, what is the dimension of the set of solutions, and which solution does np.linalg.lstsq return?

Answer

Infinitely many: M+y plus any vector of the null space, a set of dimension 29−22=7. lstsq returns the solution with the smallest norm (NumPy reference), the vector M+y that pinv also gives.

6Cholesky, Whitening and Colouring

compute a Cholesky factor by recursion, and interpret its entries as the slopes and residual standard deviations of sequential regressions
whiten and colour returns with a Cholesky factor, and explain why whitened returns have a mean squared length equal to the number of assets

The 2×2 case

LM7 classified a symmetric 2×2 matrix by completing the square, (7.4). Read as a factorization of a 2×2 covariance matrix Σ^, the completed square says

(σ^11​σ^21​​σ^21​σ^22​​)=LL⊤,L=(σ^11​​σ^21​/σ^11​​​0detΣ^/σ^11​​​).​

The factor L is lower triangular. Its diagonal is real and positive exactly when σ^11​>0 and detΣ^>0, which is LM7's test for a positive definite matrix.

The factorization

TheoremCholesky factorization

Let M be a symmetric N×N matrix. Then M is positive definite if and only if M=LL⊤ for a lower-triangular L with positive diagonal entries, and that L is unique. Proof: Deep Dive below; see also Strang (2016, §6.5) and Horn and Johnson (2013, ch. 7).

For M=Σ^, multiply out LL⊤. Entry (i,j) with i≥j is ∑p≤j​lip​ljp​=σ^ij​, and solving for the last term gives the entries column by column:

ljj​=(σ^jj​−p<j∑​ljp2​)1/2,lij​=ljj​1​(σ^ij​−p<j∑​lip​ljp​)(i>j).​(12.8)

The leading j×j block of LL⊤ uses only the leading block of L, so each leading principal minor of Σ^ is l112​⋯ljj2​. The pivots dj​ of LM9 and LM10, ratios of successive leading minors, are therefore dj​=ljj2​. If Σ^ is only semidefinite, some ljj2​ is zero or, in floating point, tiny or negative. December 2008's Σ^, 22 returns on 28 sectors, has rank 21, at most T−1 (LM10), and np.linalg.cholesky raises LinAlgError on it.

Deep DiveExistence and uniqueness of the Cholesky factoroptional · click to expand

Here x is a vector of RN, K the leading block of M of size N−1, a the rest of the last column and mNN​ the corner entry. The factor of K is LK​, and l⊤ is the last row of L without its corner.

If. When M=LL⊤ with L invertible, x⊤Mx=∥L⊤x∥2>0 for x=0.

Only if, by induction on N. For N=1 the square root of the positive entry is the only choice. For N>1 write

M=(Ka⊤​amNN​​),L=(LK​l⊤​0lNN​​).​
The block K is positive definite, so exactly one LK​ exists. The last column requires l=LK−1​a, and the corner lNN2​=mNN​−l⊤l. Take x with −K−1a above a last entry 1. Positive definiteness then gives
0<x⊤Mx​=mNN​−a⊤K−1a=mNN​−l⊤l,​
so exactly one lNN​>0 fits. ■

A chain of regressions

Each column of L has a regression meaning. Define zt​:=L−1(Rt​−Rˉ), so that Rt​−Rˉ=Lzt​. The sample covariance of zt​ is L−1Σ^L−⊤=IN​: its entries are uncorrelated, with variance 1. Row j of Lzt​ reads

Rj,t​−Rˉj​=p<j∑​ljp​zp,t​+ljj​zj,t​.

The series zp,t​ with p<j span the same space as the first j−1 centred returns, and zj,t​ is uncorrelated with them. So the sum is the least-squares fit of asset j on the assets before it, and ljj​zj,t​ is its residual. Each ljj​ is a residual standard deviation, and l11​ is the first asset's own.

Example 9Cholesky by hand for two sectors

For Semiconductor and FinancialInsurance on the full sample, σ^11​=2.323354×10−4, σ^21​=1.066603×10−4 and σ^22​=1.481729×10−4 (daily, divisor T). Compute L with (12.8) and interpret its entries.

Solution

Column 1: l11​=2.323354×10−4​=0.0152426 and l21​=1.066603×10−4/0.0152426=0.006998. Column 2: l22​=(1.481729×10−4−0.0069982)1/2=0.009960.

The ratio l21​/l11​=σ^21​/σ^11​=0.4591 is the slope of FinancialInsurance on Semiconductor. The entry l22​ is the residual standard deviation of that regression, 0.996% a day against FinancialInsurance's own 1.217%. Adding Food gives S3, whose l33​=0.008594 equals Food's residual standard deviation on the other two. Exhibit 9 gives S5's whole factor.

Whitening

The vector zt​ is the whitened return. It comes from a triangular solve of Lzt​=Rt​−Rˉ, worked down the rows, not from an inverse (on inverses, see Higham 2002a, ch. 14):

zt​=L−1(Rt​−Rˉ),T1​t∑​zt​zt⊤​=IN​,∥zt​∥2=(Rt​−Rˉ)⊤Σ^−1(Rt​−Rˉ).​(12.9)

The middle identity is L−1Σ^L−⊤=IN​, and the last uses Σ^−1=L−⊤L−1. The same factor solves a system with matrix Σ^ by two triangular solves, down the rows of L and then up those of L⊤.

Since z⊤z=tr(zz⊤) for any vector and the trace is linear,

T1​t∑​∥zt​∥2=tr(T1​t∑​zt​zt⊤​)=trIN​=N,

exactly, in every sample, with divisor T. A day with ∥zt​∥2 far above N is unusual for the joint pattern of its returns, not only for their size. Statisticians call ∥zt​∥2 the squared Mahalanobis distance (LM16). The vector zt​ depends on the order of the assets, because the order changes L; its squared length does not, by (12.9).

Example 10How unusual was 7 April 2025?

On 7 April 2025 the S5 sectors returned −9.95%, −9.89%, −8.66%, −9.90% and −9.73% (Semiconductor, FinancialInsurance, Food, Plastics, ShippingTransportation). Whiten the day with Exhibit 9's factor, and compare it with the other days.

Solution

Subtracting the sample means gives −10.048%, −9.939%, −8.693%, −9.947% and −9.772%. Forward substitution with L in % a day starts with z1​=−10.048/1.5243=−6.592, then z2​=(−9.939−0.6998z1​)/0.9960=−5.347, and continues down the rows (Exhibit 10).

The squared length is ∥z∥2=89.30, the largest of the 4,382 days, while the mean over all days is exactly 5. In the reversed order the entries change, but the squared length is again 89.30.

Exhibit 11 shows whitening for the first two sectors: a tilted elliptical cloud becomes a round one, and 7 April 2025 lies far outside both.

PitfallA capped day looks less extreme than it was

On 7 April 2025 four of the five S5 sectors fell between 9.73% and 9.95%. Each stock's daily move is limited to 10% (LM4), so a sector index cannot fall much further: the returns were capped, and 89.30 understates the shock. The day is also the extreme of the sample, so it describes the tail, not a typical day.

Colouring

Run backwards, the factor colours: if vectors z have identity sample covariance, then Lz has sample covariance LIN​L⊤=Σ^. A standard normal draw is a random number with the density φ of LM5. Applied to N independent draws, L gives a simulated vector of centred returns with covariance Σ^; LM16 and LM18 develop such simulations.

Whitening in NumPy and SciPy:

Python
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import solve_triangular

# X5: T x 5 daily returns of S5, one row per date
Xc = X5 - X5.mean(axis=0)                    # centred returns
Sigma = Xc.T @ Xc / len(Xc)                  # covariance matrix, divisor T
L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)                # lower factor
Z = solve_triangular(L, Xc.T, lower=True).T  # whitened returns, (12.9)
print((Z**2).sum(axis=1).mean())             # 5 up to rounding: N
# scipy.linalg.cholesky(Sigma) returns the upper factor, L transposed

The Polars-first notebook LM12_lab.ipynb repairs the sector closes, rebuilds the data exhibits and computational examples, and solves the computational practice problems. It ends by colouring standard normal draws with S5's L.

The notebook reads FinMind files that you download once with your own token. From the repository root, run uv run python data/fetch_finmind.py, then uv run python data/make_lab_data.py. FinMind's licence does not allow the book to redistribute the data. After that, the notebook runs offline.

導讀Cholesky 分解：把相關的報酬變成不相關

對稱矩陣（symmetric matrix）是正定（positive definite）的，若且唯若它能寫成 LL⊤，其中 L 是對角線（diagonal）為正的下三角矩陣（lower triangular matrix），而且這個 L 唯一；二階的情形就是 LM7 的配方法（completing the square）。L 的每一行都有迴歸（regression）的意義：ljj​ 是第 j 個資產對排在前面的資產迴歸後的殘差標準差（residual standard deviation）。用 L 把中心化（centring）報酬解回去，就是白化（whitening）：白化後各分量互不相關（uncorrelated）、變異數（variance）為 1，∥zt​∥2 的平均恰好等於資產個數 N。2025 年 4 月 7 日五個類股的 ∥z∥2 是 89.30，是 4,382 天中最大的一天；資產順序改變時 z 會變，長度不變，而漲跌幅限制讓這個數字低估了衝擊。反過來用 L 乘上互不相關、變異數為 1 的亂數，就是著色（colouring），可以模擬出共變異數（covariance）為 Σ^ 的報酬，留待 LM16 與 LM18 處理。

Knowledge Check 5

For S5 the mean of ∥zt​∥2 over the sample is 5. What is it for the 28 sectors of U28 on the same sample, and why is the answer exact?

Answer

The mean is 28. By the trace identity, it equals trI28​=28 for any sample whose Σ^ (divisor T) is positive definite. No model is involved: the identity holds for the data themselves.

Summary

Question Factorization Result in this module NumPy
Which constant mix of sectors best reproduces TAIEX? y=Πy+(I−Π)y last 250 returns: R-squared 0.99912, Semiconductor 0.542 lstsq, pinv
How well conditioned is the data matrix, and what is its rank? X~/T​=USV⊤ U28: κ(X~)=10.40; December 2008: rank 22 of 29 svd, cond, matrix_rank
How unusual is a day, and how are returns simulated? Σ^=LL⊤ 7 April 2025: ∥z∥2=89.30 for S5 cholesky
  • Least squares is a projection: the residual is orthogonal to every column, (12.1), and Π is symmetric and idempotent with trace N, (12.2). With an intercept, R-squared is cos2θ, (12.4).
  • TAIEX on the 28 sector indices of U28 fits the last 250 returns with R-squared 0.99912, because an accounting identity nearly holds. The coefficients are the window's best constant mix; Semiconductor's drifted from 0.189 in 2009 to 0.554 in 2026.
  • The SVD follows from the spectral theorem for M⊤M. For data λk​=sk2​, (12.5), and the normal equations square the condition number, (12.6).
  • With more coefficients than returns, every response fits exactly. The pseudoinverse (12.7) picks the minimum-norm solution; a numerical rank depends on its tolerance and scale.
  • A positive definite Σ^ has a unique Cholesky factor (12.8), a chain of regressions. Whitened returns (12.9) have identity covariance and mean squared length N.

Practice Problems

  1. Let X be a T×N matrix of rank N<T, and Π=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤. Which statement is false?

    • A.The matrix Π is symmetric.
    • B.The matrix Π is invertible.
    • C.The trace of Π equals N.

  2. TAIEX's 22 daily returns of December 2008, regressed on the 28 sector returns with an intercept, give R-squared 1 to machine precision. What does this show?

    • A.The coefficients are the market-value weights of the 28 sectors in December 2008.
    • B.The same coefficients would reproduce TAIEX's returns in January 2009.
    • C.Nothing about TAIEX: a 22×29 design of rank 22 fits any response exactly.

  3. Which of these matrices has a Cholesky factor, lower triangular with a positive diagonal?

    A: (42​25​)B: (46​69​)C: (13​34​)

    • A.Matrix A only
    • B.Matrices A and B
    • C.All three

  4. Fit a line with an intercept to the points (xt​,yt​)=(−1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(2,4). Check that the residuals sum to zero and are orthogonal to x, and compute R-squared in two ways.

  5. For x=(1,1,0)⊤, compute Π=x(x⊤x)−1x⊤, check Π2=Π and trΠ=1, and project y=(3,1,2)⊤. Is the residual orthogonal to x?

  6. Compute by hand the SVD of the matrix below, with the sign rule. Check ∣detM∣=s1​s2​, and give κ(M).

    M=(23​02​)

  7. The equations β1​+2β2​=5 and 2β1​+4β2​=10 have a coefficient matrix M of rank 1 and right-hand side y=(5,10)⊤. Find all solutions and the minimum-norm solution, and check it against M+y from (12.7).

  8. S5's singular values of X~/T​ are 0.024240, 0.013487, 0.011470, 0.009351 and 0.006964. Compute the eigenvalues of Σ^, κ(X~) and κ(Σ^), and the digits the normal equations might lose by the rule of thumb.

  9. LM7 estimated, for 0050 and 00679B, an annualized covariance matrix with σ12​=0.040425, σ22​=0.018214 and σ12​=−0.002866. Compute its Cholesky factor with 0050 first, and interpret l21​/l11​ and l22​.

  10. With the factor of Problem 9, whiten the deviation (−0.30,0.10)⊤: 0050 30 percentage points below its mean and 00679B 10 points above. Then put 00679B first and whiten again. Compare the entries and the squared lengths.

  11. (Python) Fit TAIEX's last 250 returns on U28 in three ways: lstsq on (1 X), solve on the centred normal equations (12.3), and pinv. Report R-squared, the largest gap between the slopes, κ(X~) and κ(X~⊤X~).

  12. (Python) Fit TAIEX on U28 with an intercept in each calendar year from 2009 to 2026, and report the smallest R-squared. For each year, standardize the returns of Electronic and its eight sub-industries within that year (divisor T), and compare their numerical rank at δ=0.01 with matrix_rank.

Solutions

  1. B is correct. The columns of Π lie in colX, so Π has rank N<T and is singular: it sends every residual to 0. A holds by the transpose rule, and C is (12.2).

  2. C is correct. With rank 22 equal to the number of rows, the columns span R22, so every response fits exactly. A fails because the exact fit is not unique: Example 7 finds two exact fits that disagree. B is an out-of-sample claim that no in-sample fit can support.

  3. A is correct. A Cholesky factor exists exactly when the matrix is positive definite. Matrix A has 4>0 and det=20−4=16>0; its factor has rows (2,0) and (1,2). Matrix B is positive semidefinite but singular, det=36−36=0, so the recursion gives l22​=0, not a positive number. Matrix C is indefinite, det=4−9=−5, so l222​ would be negative.

  4. The means are 0.5 and 1.5, so x~=(−1.5,−0.5,0.5,1.5)⊤ and y~​=(−1.5,−0.5,−0.5,2.5)⊤. Then β^​=6/5=1.2 and α^=1.5−1.2×0.5=0.9. The fitted values are (−0.3,0.9,2.1,3.3)⊤ and the residuals (0.3,0.1,−1.1,0.7)⊤: they sum to zero, and x⊤ε^=−0.3+0−1.1+1.4=0. R-squared is 1−1.8/9=0.8, and as a squared cosine 62/(5×9)=0.8.

  5. Since x⊤x=2, Π=xx⊤/2 has 21​ in the four entries of its leading 2×2 block and zeros elsewhere. Multiplying out confirms Π2=Π, and the trace is 21​+21​=1, the number of columns. The projection is Πy=(2,2,0)⊤, and the residual (1,−1,2)⊤ is orthogonal to x, since 1−1+0=0.

  6. Here M⊤M has rows (13,6) and (6,4), trace 17 and determinant 16, so its eigenvalues are 8.5±7.5: s1​=4 and s2​=1. The first row of M⊤M−16I is (−3,6), so v1​=(2,1)⊤/5​. The sign rule turns (1,−2)⊤/5​ into v2​=(−1,2)⊤/5​. Then u1​=Mv1​/4=(1,2)⊤/5​ and u2​=Mv2​=(−2,1)⊤/5​. Check: ∣detM∣=4=s1​s2​, and κ(M)=4.

  7. The second equation is twice the first, so the solutions are (5,0) plus any multiple of the null vector (−2,1). The one orthogonal to (−2,1) is (1,2), with norm 5​. The matrix M⊤M has eigenvalues 25 and 0, so s1​=5 and v1​=u1​=(1,2)⊤/5​. By (12.7), M+=v1​u1⊤​/5, and M+y=(1,2)⊤.

  8. The eigenvalues are λk​=sk2​: 5.876, 1.819, 1.316, 0.874 and 0.485, all times 10−4. Then κ(X~)=0.024240/0.006964=3.481 and κ(Σ^)=3.4812=12.12. Since log10​12.12=1.08, the normal equations might lose about one digit, and Exhibit 6 finds a gap below 10−14.

  9. By (12.8), l11​=0.040425​=0.20106, l21​=−0.002866/0.20106=−0.014254 and l22​=(0.018214−0.0142542)1/2=0.134204. The ratio l21​/l11​=σ12​/σ12​=−0.0709 is the slope of 00679B's returns on 0050's in LM7's sample. The entry l22​ is 00679B's volatility once the part explained by 0050 is removed: 13.42% against its own 13.50%.

  10. With 0050 first, z1​=−0.30/0.20106=−1.492 and z2​=(0.10−0.014254×1.492)/0.134204=0.587, so ∥z∥2=2.57. With 00679B first, the factor has l11​=0.018214​=0.134959, l21​=−0.002866/0.134959=−0.021236 and l22​=(0.040425−0.0212362)1/2=0.199935. Then z1​=0.10/0.134959=0.741 and z2​=(−0.30+0.021236×0.741)/0.199935=−1.422, and ∥z∥2=2.57 again: the entries differ, the squared length does not, as (12.9) requires.

  11. R-squared is 0.99912. The three slope vectors agree to better than 10−14, and κ(X~)=17.04 and κ(X~⊤X~)=290.2, as in Example 6.

  12. The smallest yearly R-squared is 0.99800, in 2021. At δ=0.01 the numerical rank of Electronic and its sub-industries is 9 in 2009, 2010 and 2018 and 8 in the other 15 years. In 2010 the ratio s9​/s1​ is 0.01004, just above the tolerance, so a slightly larger δ would give 8. matrix_rank gives 9 in all 18: its default tolerance cannot see that the nine series are nearly dependent.

Glossary

Term 中文 Meaning
Least squares 最小平方法 Choosing coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals.
Column space 行空間 All combinations Xβ of the columns of X.
Normal equations 正規方程 X⊤Xβ^​=X⊤y, (12.1): the residual is orthogonal to every column.
Projection matrix 投影矩陣 Π, (12.2): symmetric, idempotent, with trace equal to the number of columns.
Residual 殘差 ε^=y−y^​, the part of the response the fit misses.
R-squared 判定係數 Share of the centred response's squared length that a fit with an intercept reproduces, (12.4).
Singular value decomposition 奇異值分解 M=∑sk​>0​sk​uk​vk⊤​ with orthonormal uk​ and vk​ and singular values s1​≥s2​≥⋯≥0; at full column rank, M=USV⊤.
Condition number 條件數 κ(M)=s1​/sN​; forming M⊤M squares it, (12.6).
Numerical rank 數值秩 Number of singular values above δs1​, for a stated tolerance δ.
Null space 零空間 All vectors that a matrix maps to 0.
Pseudoinverse 擬反矩陣 M+=∑sk​>0​vk​uk⊤​/sk​, (12.7); M+y is the minimum-norm least-squares solution.
Cholesky factorization Cholesky 分解 Σ^=LL⊤ with L lower triangular with a positive diagonal, (12.8).
Whitening 白化 zt​=L−1(Rt​−Rˉ), (12.9): uncorrelated entries with variance 1.
Colouring 著色 Lz: vectors with identity covariance turned into vectors with covariance Σ^.
